Covid-19 - One year on

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We reflect on a year of Covid-19.. How has it changed our lives?

Unique Selling Point:
On 5 March 2020 the first case of Covid-19 was diagnosed in South Africa. Within 3 weeks the country went into hard lockdown and our lives changed forever, but at the same time, life has continued… people have had to carry on without loved ones, learners have had to continue schooling under difficult circumstances, health workers have had to show up for work, sometimes without the correct PPE, during scary times when more than 13,000 Covid-19 patients lay in hospital beds across the country. We don’t know what the future has in store for us, how the virus will continue to alter the world… but we can reflect on everything we’ve been through and perhaps this will give us hope for the future…

Summary:
We look back at the past 12 months of living with a global pandemic, and we revisit some of the people we met along the way. Was it as bad as people had expected? How did their lives change? What are their hopes for the future?
We will touch base with Gift of the Givers who spent much time on the forefront of this pandemic, mothers who have had babies in lockdown, couples who found love and navigated relationships. We will also speak to some experts who can summarise how our world has changed over the past year - FEDHASA on on the hospitality industry in SA, economist Duma Gqubule who will convey the impacts on the economy and Francois Venter will speak about the impacts on our healthcare system... Interweaved with updates from case studies as highlighted below.

Further information:
One year later, South Africa has had about 1.55 million cases on Covid-19 — officially — and over 52,000 people have died from the virus. But besides the direct impact of Covid, it is perhaps the indirect impact that has hit us the hardest.

* Our GDP slumped by 7% in 2020
*Estimated R285 billion reduction in tax revenue collected in 2020. (that’s more than our entire health budget for 2020/21)

* There has been a 7.1% increase in business insolvencies in Jan 2021 compared to Jan 2020.
* In the fourth quarter of 2020 income from tourism accommodation dropped by 57.7% and this increased to a whopping 72.9% in Jan/Feb 2021
* Similarly 2020 Q4 showed a 28.2% decline compared to the same period in 2019 by the food and beverage industry… During the first quarter of 2021 this decline went up to 36.1%
— These stats are from the Federated Hospitality Association of SA (Rosemary Anderson) — stating that the situation could be much worse as many small businesses have fallen through the cracks.

* About 2million learners did not return to school after lockdown. — 15%

* Maternal Mortality Rate went up by 30% during April to Sept 2020
* There was a 20% increase in stll births in Mpumalanga during April to Sept 2020
* There was increased pressure on rural healthcare facilities as many people moved out of the cities for lockdown.
* research shows that there were about 200,000 less contraceptive visits to clinics and doctors in Quarter 2 & 3 of 2020.
* There were about 8,000 less termination of pregnancies…
* 23% of babies delivered we below birth weight
* Interestingly there were more births in facilities in 2020 compared to 2019, but pregnant women went for their 1st antenatal checkups much later (on average) than in previous years.

TB tests done dropped by about 50,000 tests per week for Lockdown level 5 and 4 in 2020.
It is estimated that curtailing HIV services in South Africa will result in 1000x more deaths than what covid has produced. In other words, if patients do not have access to HIV anti-retrovirals we will end up with 500,000 excess deaths a year, in stead of the 50,000 from the coronavirus.

The fact is that Covid has had a massive effect on our world. As part of the “update” we will go back to some of the case studies we spoke to during the year.

Andrew McPherson - One of the first patients diagnosed with Covid-19
One year later he has actually had Covid-19 twice now.. and still cannot smell.

Thato Moloko - Baragwanath Emergency Unit
Life has calmed down considerably - They are bracing themselves for the third wave

Tom Boyles - Infectious Disease Expert
Moved to rural Eastern Cape - expert in HIV care, focussing on that instead of Covid-19

Marcelle Roberts - Durban Chef
— Closed their restaurants and opted to open a smaller venue (all-in one), no more fine dining, just good food and cold beer. They had to let go a lot of staff as a result. They had good turnover in November before the second wave. Trying to push takeaways and doing some additional marketing like Happy Hours etc to keep the business alive.

Wandile Mabaso - Jhb Chef
— They did deliveries but struggled because of the lack of control over quality of the food. They started sending private chefs to homes for special events and then even placed some chefs in permanent positions. they also did virtual dinners, sending chefs to several homes at the same time and guiding diners through the experience via Zoom.

Morag Maynard - Owner: Zoo Lake Sports Club — Closed down in January. Could not make ends meet, especially after the second wave when all sports at Zoo Lake was cancelled. No insurance relief.

Kim Whitaker - Ubunthu Beds
Kim contracted Covid in March 2020, and she started an NGO called Ubuntu beds. She has about 700 hotels and B&B's offering free accommodation to field workers so they can be closer to hospitals. This operation is going very well. Essential Healthcare workers from all over the country are benefitting from this. They are able to stay closer to work, and also keep their loved ones safe.

Robyn Jansen van Vuuren & Tshiwela Makhwathana - New Moms
— They both have happy bouncy babies. Still recovering from the trauma of the births but all good and healthy and happy. Robyn says having a baby is a busy job, and means that you don’t get much time to dwell on the past. Tshiwela says childcare has been an issue, not easy to keep a baby safe in these times.

Bertram Malgas and Monique Mortlock - Couple in love - were supposed to get married in 2020 They are still together. Agreed to spend hard lockdown apart to keep each other safe. They have seen each other since. It has been hard, but they are determined to make it work. They have not yet set a date to marry, but are determined to do so eventually.

Michelle and Dan - Got engaged in 2020 during lockdown It was tough on them financially, but Michelle started a new job in Dec 2020 and now things are better again.. Still in love, and will get married when the pandemic has calmed down.

Press Release:


COVID-19 – One Year On

After a year of unparalleled tribulation with the country in the grip of a global pandemic, Carte Blanche recaps what happened to people featured in nearly 50 stories from the past year who were simply trying to make the best of a bad situation. We went from the first shocks of having to close businesses as lockdown hit hard, to birthing new life in isolation without partners by their side, and following frontline workers struggling on the job, in the face of the unknown, without sleep as patients battled the disease and its long-term impact. We unpacked the science as it developed and the politics of coming to terms with the disease and treatments, all while trying to find reasons to hope. Now, we celebrate the grit and tenacity of some amazing South Africans that survived and thrived.

Producer: Stenette Grosskopf | Presenter: Claire Mawisa



Script:


Covid One Year SCRIPT


LINK
It's hard to imagine that this was our lives less than 18 months ago... and I'm not talking about the rugby... I’m talking about filled stadiums with strangers standing shoulder to shoulder, packed restaurants, no mask in sight.. And people high-fiving and even hugging! But 2020 changed all of that.
V/O
Since early last year we’ve been documenting the impacts of Covid-19 on our lives. We’ve spoken to survivors, the heroes on the frontlines, the innovators and the vulnerable, sharing stories of bravery and loss.
UPSOUND
Thato Moloko: You also realize you’re more human than you would like to believe.
Robyn Jansen van Vuuren: It really was my worst nightmare to give birth alone.
James Diack: We’re all uncertain, we don’t know where this ends.
V/O
More than a year of lockdown, travel restrictions and financial hardship have made life challenging for everyone and the tourism and food & beverage industries were hit hard.
LINK
Unfortunately like so many restaurants across the country, even popular well-established ones could not survive the last year.
V/O
Business interruption insurance was meant to be a lifeline in case of unforeseen disasters, but some claimants found that it was almost impossible to meet qualifying criteria.
Scott Cochrane
For our cover to kick in the viral threat would have to originate at our business.
V/O
For the past twelve months, Scott Cochrane’s guesthouse in Pretoria has been mostly empty.
Scott Cochrane
I have been without an income basically for a year and really have been having to be innovative to survive.
V/O
Fed up, he took his case to the Ombudsman and after a year-long battle and a mountain of paperwork, he finally did get an insurance payout.
Scott Cochrane
At least it’s a bit of relief. It can keep us going while we make plans to reopen and get going, you know...
James Diack
If I look at the tally of what lockdown was for me, I lost three restaurants, I had to relocate one, and improvisation has been the name of the game
V/O
When Joburg restaurateur James Diack closed his doors at the beginning of lockdown last year he had no idea what the future would bring.
James Diack
Claire: So James, the last time I saw you, you were actually locking the restaurant because lockdown was going to start the following day. How have the last twelve months been?

Look, the last twelve months has been a proper rocky ride. The last time you saw me leave that restaurant was the last time we left that restaurant. We never reopened or re-operated down there.
V/O
While some businesses managed to return to a new normal after the initial Lockdown restrictions were lifted, Diack says it was a slow recovery for his eateries and finally at the beginning of December he managed to reopen his trademark restaurant at a new location in Joburg.
James Diack
We had to literally creep, creep back into it and still as we sit today we’re still only running at 60%.

Claire: Status of cashflow right now.

Uhmm, status of cashflow is we can pay our suppliers today. And we’ll hopefully have a busy night and we can pay some more suppliers tomorrow.
LINK
Everyone is struggling. Economists estimate that more than 500,000 formal jobs have been lost since 2019 and our GDP has slumped by 7%.
Dr Sooliman
Immediately after the lockdown, three weeks later, a massive hunger started in the country.
V/O
Founder of the humanitarian organisation Gift of the Givers -- Dr Imtiaaz Sooliman -- has first-hand knowledge of the desperate situation many South Africans found themselves in.
Dr Sooliman
A mother takes a food parcel and then she says thank you very much for this, but talk to my children. They will tell you the taste of every plant in this area. Last year they were eating tortoises, lizards and frogs.
V/O
Over the past year Gift of the Givers set up over 100 feeding centres around the country, and they have been tirelessly handing out hundreds of thousands of food parcels to assist the most vulnerable.
Dr Sooliman
Claire: Physically, mentally emotionally you guys have been busy, you’re on the ground, you’re on the frontline...How are you doing?
Claire, It may seem strange… my teams are built for this. You can’t stop them, you can’t hold them back. They’ve worked, without exaggeration, from the 15th of March to today without a single day’s break.
V/O
Besides feeding people and tirelessly providing water to drought-stricken communities, GOTG has been at the forefront of supplying PPE and equipment to under resourced hospitals and clinics.
Dr Thato Moloko
It’s gotten to a point where we choose who’s worth a resuss attempt or we choose who’s worth oxygen.
V/O
We first met Dr Thato Moloko in August last year when she filmed a video diary of her life at the Baragwanath Medical Emergency Unit during the first wave.
Dr Thato Moloko
Claire: What came out in the story that you did is that there was not enough… of everything… Did it get worse than what we saw?
Yes, so second wave was maybe not as many numbers but we were seeing worse cases. So ICU got full. We ran out of oxygen, we ran out of supply… and now you have someone who not only requires oxygen, but requires intubation and we do not have anything.
Claire: What then happens?
You document and you pray and you call and you ask. You use it for this long and then you stop and you use it here and the resource problem has not gotten better. We ran out of swabs at one point.
V/O
Even at the outset of the pandemic it became clear that medical professionals on the frontline would need additional support, and when Kim Whitaker was diagnosed as Patient Number 42 in March last year, she had a light-bulb moment.
Kim Whitaker
I thought oh maybe we could build a platform to connect healthcare workers to empty hotels. I called a friend of mine in Johannesburg, I said I wanna launch it on Monday morning. And he was like, my team’s so keen. We’re gonna do it.
LINK
This is one hotel of over a thousand that are part of the Ubuntu Beds network, an initiative started to support healthcare workers.
V/O
To date almost 30,000 nights have been booked, giving over a thousand doctors and nurses a home-away-from-home. And there are plans to expand the platform, to assist in other disasters.
Kim Whitaker
What we have trialed so far is … what would it look like if we used our platform for example in the case of a township fire. So in Gugulethu there was a township fire about six months ago we had about twenty families displaced and within 3 hours we had them placed in a guesthouse. And so we’re hoping that we’re gonna be able to use the technology that was built to help people in need in future and to keep the spirit of Ubuntu alive, really.
LINK
The pandemic has also interrupted the healthcare sector indirectly, disrupting services like routine immunisations and according to experts maternal mortality increased by 30% between April and September 2020.
LINK
Late last year I met some mothers who shared their lockdown birthing experiences and finally I get to meet the bundle of joy.
V/O
Robyn Jansen van Vuuren went into premature labour during lockdown and because of Covid protocols, she ended up giving birth alone, without the support of her husband.
Robyn Jansen van Rensburg
It was so sudden. The nurses and the doctors wheeled me into theatre in full protective gear...
V/O
Allegra is almost a year old and already quite familiar with zoom calls, as you can see!
UPSOUND
Robyn Jansen van Vuuren
She’s unlikely to cooperate.

Claire: That was the brief.

Oh good.

She’s following the brief to the tee.
Robyn Jansen van Vuuren
Claire: As a mother, have you been okay? Because it’s tough as a new mother…

Absolutely… I think that we definitely became a lot more proficient at parenting more quickly than perhaps we would have under other circumstances.

Claire: On reflection, when you think about your birth story what do you think?

It is just the way she came into the world. I have nothing to compare it to and the experience bought me my daughter who is just the most amazing little bundle of energy and joy and light...
V/O
Tshiwela Makhwathana’s son, Zacharia was also born in lockdown. Although the initial experience was somewhat traumatic, she says the family is healthy and happy and she sent me some pictures.
Tshiwela Makhwathana
It is such a joy and blessing to have him in our family as my other two enjoy having him around,
V/O
As we move into the second year of the global pandemic, there is an air of hopefulness as vaccine programmes are being rolled out and people are slowly rebuilding their lives.
James Diack
Claire: What were some of the lessons learnt that will change the way you do business perhaps forever…?

Diversify. Don’t have all your eggs in one basket and then to try and be the best because people are really short of cash. So if people are going to choose an amazing, one spoil a month, we have to be that person.




Claire: Was there any point during this journey where you think I just want to opt out…
Yes, multiple times. It’s when you are at work and you’re pushing, and what you’re doing is not enough and somebody still dies. Or you have to let them die because there’s nowhere else for them to go, there’s no ICU bed. Those are moments when I have been like… I cannot. I can’t watch the news. I can’t look at the numbers anymore. I just look at the survivors, the preventions. We could’ve lost this patient, but we did good. We saved this patient's life today. And I might have lost 5 today but I saved one.






PROMO 1
From brave healthcare workers and real-life heroes to anxious new mothers and struggling business owners… We look back at some of the stories from the past year of living in a global pandemic.




PROMO 2
After more than a year of documenting the impacts of Covid-19 we look back and revisit some of the people we met along the way to see how they have weathered the storm.




PROMO 3
The Covid-19 pandemic has taken a toll on our economy, healthcare sector and society… We revisit some of the people we met over the past year, sharing stories of hope.

We unpacked the science as it developed and the politics of coming to terms with the disease and treatments, all while trying to find reasons to hope. Now, we celebrate the grit and tenacity of some amazing South Africans that survived and thrived. Producer: Stenette Grosskopf | Presenter: Claire Mawisa Script: Covid One Year SCRIPT LINK It's hard to imagine that this was our lives less than 18 months ago... and I'm not talking about the rugby... I’m talking about filled stadiums with strangers standing shoulder to shoulder, packed restaurants, no mask in sight.. And people high-fiving and even hugging! But 2020 changed all of that. V/O Since early last year we’ve been documenting the impacts of Covid-19 on our lives. We’ve spoken to survivors, the heroes on the frontlines, the innovators and the vulnerable, sharing stories of bravery and loss. UPSOUND Thato Moloko: You also realize you’re more human than you would like to believe. Robyn Jansen van Vuuren: It really was my worst nightmare to give birth alone. James Diack: We’re all uncertain, we don’t know where this ends. V/O More than a year of lockdown, travel restrictions and financial hardship have made life challenging for everyone and the tourism and food & beverage industries were hit hard. LINK Unfortunately like so many restaurants across the country, even popular well-established ones could not survive the last year. V/O Business interruption insurance was meant to be a lifeline in case of unforeseen disasters, but some claimants found that it was almost impossible to meet qualifying criteria. Scott Cochrane For our cover to kick in the viral threat would have to originate at our business. V/O For the past twelve months, Scott Cochrane’s guesthouse in Pretoria has been mostly empty. Scott Cochrane I have been without an income basically for a year and really have been having to be innovative to survive. V/O Fed up, he took his case to the Ombudsman and after a year-long battle and a mountain of paperwork, he finally did get an insurance payout. Scott Cochrane At least it’s a bit of relief. It can keep us going while we make plans to reopen and get going, you know... James Diack If I look at the tally of what lockdown was for me, I lost three restaurants, I had to relocate one, and improvisation has been the name of the game V/O When Joburg restaurateur James Diack closed his doors at the beginning of lockdown last year he had no idea what the future would bring. James Diack Claire: So James, the last time I saw you, you were actually locking the restaurant because lockdown was going to start the following day. How have the last twelve months been? Look, the last twelve months has been a proper rocky ride. The last time you saw me leave that restaurant was the last time we left that restaurant. We never reopened or re-operated down there. V/O While some businesses managed to return to a new normal after the initial Lockdown restrictions were lifted, Diack says it was a slow recovery for his eateries and finally at the beginning of December he managed to reopen his trademark restaurant at a new location in Joburg. James Diack We had to literally creep, creep back into it and still as we sit today we’re still only running at 60%. Claire: Status of cashflow right now. Uhmm, status of cashflow is we can pay our suppliers today. And we’ll hopefully have a busy night and we can pay some more suppliers tomorrow. LINK Everyone is struggling. Economists estimate that more than 500,000 formal jobs have been lost since 2019 and our GDP has slumped by 7%. Dr Sooliman Immediately after the lockdown, three weeks later, a massive hunger started in the country. V/O Founder of the humanitarian organisation Gift of the Givers -- Dr Imtiaaz Sooliman -- has first-hand knowledge of the desperate situation many South Africans found themselves in. Dr Sooliman A mother takes a food parcel and then she says thank you very much for this, but talk to my children. They will tell you the taste of every plant in this area. Last year they were eating tortoises, lizards and frogs. V/O Over the past year Gift of the Givers set up over 100 feeding centres around the country, and they have been tirelessly handing out hundreds of thousands of food parcels to assist the most vulnerable. Dr Sooliman Claire: Physically, mentally emotionally you guys have been busy, you’re on the ground, you’re on the frontline...How are you doing? Claire, It may seem strange… my teams are built for this. You can’t stop them, you can’t hold them back. They’ve worked, without exaggeration, from the 15th of March to today without a single day’s break. V/O Besides feeding people and tirelessly providing water to drought-stricken communities, GOTG has been at the forefront of supplying PPE and equipment to under resourced hospitals and clinics. Dr Thato Moloko It’s gotten to a point where we choose who’s worth a resuss attempt or we choose who’s worth oxygen. V/O We first met Dr Thato Moloko in August last year when she filmed a video diary of her life at the Baragwanath Medical Emergency Unit during the first wave. Dr Thato Moloko Claire: What came out in the story that you did is that there was not enough… of everything… Did it get worse than what we saw? Yes, so second wave was maybe not as many numbers but we were seeing worse cases. So ICU got full. We ran out of oxygen, we ran out of supply… and now you have someone who not only requires oxygen, but requires intubation and we do not have anything. Claire: What then happens? You document and you pray and you call and you ask. You use it for this long and then you stop and you use it here and the resource problem has not gotten better. We ran out of swabs at one point. V/O Even at the outset of the pandemic it became clear that medical professionals on the frontline would need additional support, and when Kim Whitaker was diagnosed as Patient Number 42 in March last year, she had a light-bulb moment. Kim Whitaker I thought oh maybe we could build a platform to connect healthcare workers to empty hotels. I called a friend of mine in Johannesburg, I said I wanna launch it on Monday morning. And he was like, my team’s so keen. We’re gonna do it. LINK This is one hotel of over a thousand that are part of the Ubuntu Beds network, an initiative started to support healthcare workers. V/O To date almost 30,000 nights have been booked, giving over a thousand doctors and nurses a home-away-from-home. And there are plans to expand the platform, to assist in other disasters. Kim Whitaker What we have trialed so far is … what would it look like if we used our platform for example in the case of a township fire. So in Gugulethu there was a township fire about six months ago we had about twenty families displaced and within 3 hours we had them placed in a guesthouse. And so we’re hoping that we’re gonna be able to use the technology that was built to help people in need in future and to keep the spirit of Ubuntu alive, really. LINK The pandemic has also interrupted the healthcare sector indirectly, disrupting services like routine immunisations and according to experts maternal mortality increased by 30% between April and September 2020. LINK Late last year I met some mothers who shared their lockdown birthing experiences and finally I get to meet the bundle of joy. V/O Robyn Jansen van Vuuren went into premature labour during lockdown and because of Covid protocols, she ended up giving birth alone, without the support of her husband. Robyn Jansen van Rensburg It was so sudden. The nurses and the doctors wheeled me into theatre in full protective gear... V/O Allegra is almost a year old and already quite familiar with zoom calls, as you can see! UPSOUND Robyn Jansen van Vuuren She’s unlikely to cooperate. Claire: That was the brief. Oh good. She’s following the brief to the tee. Robyn Jansen van Vuuren Claire: As a mother, have you been okay? Because it’s tough as a new mother… Absolutely… I think that we definitely became a lot more proficient at parenting more quickly than perhaps we would have under other circumstances. Claire: On reflection, when you think about your birth story what do you think? It is just the way she came into the world. I have nothing to compare it to and the experience bought me my daughter who is just the most amazing little bundle of energy and joy and light... V/O Tshiwela Makhwathana’s son, Zacharia was also born in lockdown. Although the initial experience was somewhat traumatic, she says the family is healthy and happy and she sent me some pictures. Tshiwela Makhwathana It is such a joy and blessing to have him in our family as my other two enjoy having him around, V/O As we move into the second year of the global pandemic, there is an air of hopefulness as vaccine programmes are being rolled out and people are slowly rebuilding their lives. James Diack Claire: What were some of the lessons learnt that will change the way you do business perhaps forever…? Diversify. Don’t have all your eggs in one basket and then to try and be the best because people are really short of cash. So if people are going to choose an amazing, one spoil a month, we have to be that person. Claire: Was there any point during this journey where you think I just want to opt out… Yes, multiple times. It’s when you are at work and you’re pushing, and what you’re doing is not enough and somebody still dies. Or you have to let them die because there’s nowhere else for them to go, there’s no ICU bed. Those are moments when I have been like… I cannot. I can’t watch the news. I can’t look at the numbers anymore. I just look at the survivors, the preventions. We could’ve lost this patient, but we did good. We saved this patient's life today. And I might have lost 5 today but I saved one. PROMO 2 After more than a year of documenting the impacts of Covid-19 we look back and revisit some of the people we met along the way to see how they have weathered the storm. PROMO 3 The Covid-19 pandemic has taken a toll on our economy, healthcare sector and society… We revisit some of the people we met over the past year, sharing stories of hope.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We reflect on a year of Covid-19.. How has it changed our lives?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: On 5 March 2020 the first case of Covid-19 was diagnosed in South Africa. Within 3 weeks the country went into hard lockdown and our lives changed forever, but at the same time, life has continued… people have had to carry on without loved ones, learners have had to continue schooling under difficult circumstances, health workers have had to show up for work, sometimes without the correct PPE, during scary times when more than 13,000 Covid-19 patients lay in hospital beds across the country. We don’t know what the future has in store for us, how the virus will continue to alter the world… but we can reflect on everything we’ve been through and perhaps this will give us hope for the future…
metadata.Summary: We look back at the past 12 months of living with a global pandemic, and we revisit some of the people we met along the way. Was it as bad as people had expected? How did their lives change? What are their hopes for the future? We will touch base with Gift of the Givers who spent much time on the forefront of this pandemic, mothers who have had babies in lockdown, couples who found love and navigated relationships. We will also speak to some experts who can summarise how our world has changed over the past year - FEDHASA on on the hospitality industry in SA, economist Duma Gqubule who will convey the impacts on the economy and Francois Venter will speak about the impacts on our healthcare system... Interweaved with updates from case studies as highlighted below.
metadata.Further information: One year later, South Africa has had about 1.55 million cases on Covid-19 — officially — and over 52,000 people have died from the virus. But besides the direct impact of Covid, it is perhaps the indirect impact that has hit us the hardest. * Our GDP slumped by 7% in 2020 *Estimated R285 billion reduction in tax revenue collected in 2020. (that’s more than our entire health budget for 2020/21) * There has been a 7.1% increase in business insolvencies in Jan 2021 compared to Jan 2020. * In the fourth quarter of 2020 income from tourism accommodation dropped by 57.7% and this increased to a whopping 72.9% in Jan/Feb 2021 * Similarly 2020 Q4 showed a 28.2% decline compared to the same period in 2019 by the food and beverage industry… During the first quarter of 2021 this decline went up to 36.1% — These stats are from the Federated Hospitality Association of SA (Rosemary Anderson) — stating that the situation could be much worse as many small businesses have fallen through the cracks. * About 2million learners did not return to school after lockdown. — 15% * Maternal Mortality Rate went up by 30% during April to Sept 2020 * There was a 20% increase in stll births in Mpumalanga during April to Sept 2020 * There was increased pressure on rural healthcare facilities as many people moved out of the cities for lockdown. * research shows that there were about 200,000 less contraceptive visits to clinics and doctors in Quarter 2 & 3 of 2020. * There were about 8,000 less termination of pregnancies… * 23% of babies delivered we below birth weight * Interestingly there were more births in facilities in 2020 compared to 2019, but pregnant women went for their 1st antenatal checkups much later (on average) than in previous years. TB tests done dropped by about 50,000 tests per week for Lockdown level 5 and 4 in 2020. It is estimated that curtailing HIV services in South Africa will result in 1000x more deaths than what covid has produced. In other words, if patients do not have access to HIV anti-retrovirals we will end up with 500,000 excess deaths a year, in stead of the 50,000 from the coronavirus. The fact is that Covid has had a massive effect on our world. As part of the “update” we will go back to some of the case studies we spoke to during the year. Andrew McPherson - One of the first patients diagnosed with Covid-19 One year later he has actually had Covid-19 twice now.. and still cannot smell. Thato Moloko - Baragwanath Emergency Unit Life has calmed down considerably - They are bracing themselves for the third wave Tom Boyles - Infectious Disease Expert Moved to rural Eastern Cape - expert in HIV care, focussing on that instead of Covid-19 Marcelle Roberts - Durban Chef — Closed their restaurants and opted to open a smaller venue (all-in one), no more fine dining, just good food and cold beer. They had to let go a lot of staff as a result. They had good turnover in November before the second wave. Trying to push takeaways and doing some additional marketing like Happy Hours etc to keep the business alive. Wandile Mabaso - Jhb Chef — They did deliveries but struggled because of the lack of control over quality of the food. They started sending private chefs to homes for special events and then even placed some chefs in permanent positions. they also did virtual dinners, sending chefs to several homes at the same time and guiding diners through the experience via Zoom. Morag Maynard - Owner: Zoo Lake Sports Club — Closed down in January. Could not make ends meet, especially after the second wave when all sports at Zoo Lake was cancelled. No insurance relief. Kim Whitaker - Ubunthu Beds Kim contracted Covid in March 2020, and she started an NGO called Ubuntu beds. She has about 700 hotels and B&B's offering free accommodation to field workers so they can be closer to hospitals. This operation is going very well. Essential Healthcare workers from all over the country are benefitting from this. They are able to stay closer to work, and also keep their loved ones safe. Robyn Jansen van Vuuren & Tshiwela Makhwathana - New Moms — They both have happy bouncy babies. Still recovering from the trauma of the births but all good and healthy and happy. Robyn says having a baby is a busy job, and means that you don’t get much time to dwell on the past. Tshiwela says childcare has been an issue, not easy to keep a baby safe in these times. Bertram Malgas and Monique Mortlock - Couple in love - were supposed to get married in 2020 They are still together. Agreed to spend hard lockdown apart to keep each other safe. They have seen each other since. It has been hard, but they are determined to make it work. They have not yet set a date to marry, but are determined to do so eventually. Michelle and Dan - Got engaged in 2020 during lockdown It was tough on them financially, but Michelle started a new job in Dec 2020 and now things are better again.. Still in love, and will get married when the pandemic has calmed down.
